text:
## Observations

1. Sorting the paired values \((A_i, B_i)\) by \(A_i\) makes the indices with \(A_i \le a\) a prefix for every distinct value \(a\).
2. For a threshold \(a\) with at least \(K\) eligible indices, the smallest possible sum is the sum of the \(K\) smallest eligible \(B_i\) values. A max-heap of size at most \(K\) can maintain those values as the prefix grows.
3. Every threshold product is at least the true optimum, and the threshold equal to an optimal subset’s maximum \(A_i\) gives a product at most the true optimum.
4. Since \(1 \le K \le N\), the last threshold always yields a candidate. Each pair enters the heap once and causes at most one removal.

## Solution sketch

1. “Sorting the paired values \((A_i, B_i)\) by \(A_i\) makes the indices with \(A_i \le a\) a prefix for every distinct value \(a\).”  
   For each test case, pair the values by their original indices and sort the pairs by \(A_i\). Process all pairs with the same \(A_i\) together so that, after each group, the prefix contains every index eligible at that threshold.

2. “For a threshold \(a\) with at least \(K\) eligible indices, the smallest possible sum is the sum of the \(K\) smallest eligible \(B_i\) values. A max-heap of size at most \(K\) can maintain those values as the prefix grows.”  
   Insert each \(B_i\) into the heap and add it to a running sum. Whenever the heap grows beyond \(K\), remove its largest value and subtract it from the sum. After each group, evaluate \(a\) times the running sum if the heap contains \(K\) values.

3. “Every threshold product is at least the true optimum, and the threshold equal to an optimal subset’s maximum \(A_i\) gives a product at most the true optimum.”  
   Keep the smallest product and print it for the test case. The heap’s selected indices form a valid subset whose actual maximum is at most \(a\). Since the sum is positive, its actual objective is at most the threshold product. At the threshold given by an optimal subset’s maximum, that subset is eligible, so the heap’s sum is at most its sum. These two bounds establish that the smallest threshold product equals the optimum.

4. “Since \(1 \le K \le N\), the last threshold always yields a candidate. Each pair enters the heap once and causes at most one removal.”  
   The same scan handles \(K=1\), when the heap keeps one value, and \(K=N\), when the only candidate comes after the final group. Equal \(B_i\) values are handled as separate heap entries. Per test case, sorting takes \(O(N\log N)\) time and the heap takes \(O(N\log(K+1))\) time. The sorted pairs and heap use \(O(N+K)=O(N)\) space.
